Image credit: Nintendo News by Dom Peppiatt Deputy Editorial Director Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 2:10 p.m. 12 comments Follow The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild Prioritise us on Google Today, during a Nintendo Direct dedicated to the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda series, Columbia Pictures and Nintendo released the first-ever trailer for the upcoming live-action The Legend of Zelda movie, starring Bo Bragason as the titular Princess Zelda and Benjamin Evan Ainsworth as Link.
When we see the film, apparently, we'll understand why there isn't a subtitle, says Miyamoto during the Direct. He then asks us what role we think the Triforce will play? Apparently, the film will draw on all elements of the 40-year history of the series to date, but beyond that there is not much we know about the film. It seems the movie will not be based on any one single game, however. More news is coming at a later date, including - we should hope - a trailer.
What else do we know about The Legend of Zelda live-action movie adaptation? Well, we know the initial shoot has wrapped filming in New Zealand (after starting the shoot in October 2025), and we know that Wes Ball - of Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes and Maze Runner fame - is directing. We know it's going to get a theatrical run, but then will stream on Netflix at an as-yet-undisclosed time after the initial release.
If you're keen to see the young stars at the centre of this film in something else to tide you over until release, Benjamin Evan Ainsworth took on a fairly big role in House of the Dragon Season 3, playing Daeron Targaryen in a season that really showed his acting chops as the Targaryen began to crumble in earnest.
If you want to feel old, Ainsworth was only eight when Breath of the Wild released. The young actor will be 18 when the film launches on 30th April, 2027, though - somehow making it 10 years since the Nintendo Switch game first launched.

It's a thorny question, and one that's been the subject of a lot of internet debate since Persona 4 Revival - a remake of the 2008 original - was revealed. To cut a long story short, a lot of people see Persona 4 as problematic. One of the main cast, Yosuke, is a conservative, judgemental, 'teenage pervert' stereotype. While he does have an arc that sees him soften somewhat, he's also just a bit of an asshole. Elsewhere in the game, there are allusions to gay and trans storylines some feel are inelegantly handled - where the characters in question can be seen to suppress their true selves for the sake of 'falling in line' with what society expects.
I think there's more nuance to these storylines than the more rabid subreddit discussions would have you believe, and that some of the game's core crew do actually internalise their more complex traits and process their shame as the game progresses - but I will concede these issues are handled in an often cack-handed way. Throw in some clumsy comments from the series director about how restoring one homosexual romance would require that the main character be able to romance "all the guys", too, and you can see why there's a lot of indignation about the handling of Persona 4's more sensitive topics.
At Gamescom, I had the chance to sit down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about this, and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake. Half the fanbase doesn't want the developer to interfere with the 2008 release at all, whilst the other half wants Atlus to take a good hard look at what it's done in the past and, simply, do better. To Wada, it seems, a lot of the solution lies in localisation.
"When it comes down to it, we didn't really change the core of any character," he tells me, via interpreter. "The characters are still who they are, saying what they're saying. One thing that we did realise, though, was that when we originally wrote the game, some of the lines weren't very clear, lacked information, or the way that we phrased them wasn't very effective at portraying the character in the way that we wanted to portray. So we did go and revisit that, and we tweaked little bits and bobs to make sure it's clear what the character's intention was. In terms of Yosuke specifically, everything he's saying is the same, but we just made a couple parts a little bit more gentle." Will this be enough to placate Western audiences and address some of the more problematic elements of the script? It remains to be seen.
From this line of conversation, we go on to talk about the localisation process and how it's changed at Atlus over the years. It used to be that Atlus games would release in Japan first, before pivoting to work on localised versions of its games to launch into the global market: Persona 5, for instance, debuted in Japan in September 2016, but did not release globally until April 2017. However, with the worldwide - and mainstream - success of Persona 5, Atlus modified its approach and began doing simultaneous global releases. Metaphor Refantazio, Persona 3 Reload and Shin Megami Tensei 5: Vengeance have all benefited from this new way of working. Notably, Persona 3 Reload would go on to be Atlus' fastest-selling game, ever.
"With Persona 3 Reload, it was our first time doing a simultaneous release - and from that game, we learned a lot about the overall process," says Wada. "So this time, when we were creating the game from the beginning, we put a lot of effort into ensuring we could get the best-quality localisations as quickly as we could. Once we had a scenario finished or completed a part of a script - as soon as we could - we'd pass it to the localisation teams, let them work their magic, and make it so that everyone was on the same page and working in unison. We made sure to have them in the room when you're having discussions very early so that we could very quickly and very effectively work closely with them." Wada hopes the resulting script is something that is more holistic, and better reflects the developer's intent, even in languages it is not originally produced in.
Additionally, he notes the characters have become more mature since the release of the original Persona 4 thanks to titles like Persona 4: Dancing All Night and the two fighting games Persona 4 Arena and Persona 4 Arena Ultimax. While these games occur after the events of Persona 4, Wada says the extra work done on developing the characters post-game helped provide more depth and substance for their appearance in Revival.
"In a lot of ways, there has been something more we could explore with every character. Since Persona 4 came out, there have been a number of spin-off games that have been released, where we developed the characters and their personalities. So when we were making Revival, we took aspects of that and helped it to inform our characters and add detail and depth. For the team, it was Yosuke and Kanji that they really wanted to explore and go more in-depth with."
"In going back to Persona 4," adds art director Akane Kabayashi, "I realised that Chie is forced to wear a lot of different hats and do a lot of different things. You can see that Chie and Yukiko are like 'double heroines', but Chie is given a lot more stuff to do than Yukiko is, and it made me really respect that aspect of her."
I'm intrigued to see how Wada and Atlus manage to toe the line between faithful remake and updated revision when it comes to Revival. The team's past remake, Persona 3 Reload, corrected a lot of the mistakes present in both the original game and the Portable remake - but it still made some of those classic cack-handed moves in its marketing and production. I'm worried Persona 4 Revival is cursed to suffer the same fate, but I'm hoping that the final release of the game makes good on at least some of the improvements Wada seems keen to implement.

Image credit: Nintendo News by Robert Purchese Associate Editor Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 11:53 a.m. 119 comments Follow Legend of Zelda Prioritise us on Google The first of two Nintendo Direct showcases airs today, this one themed around The Legend of Zelda, which turned 40 years old this year. And we'll be covering it live, right here, as it happens.
The show starts 3pm UK time and lasts for roughly 30 minutes, Nintendo has said, and contains "a variety of The Legend of Zelda-related information about the series' 40th anniversary". Exactly what that means, we don't yet know, but we can make a couple of educated guesses.
Guess number one: a release date and proper reveal for the Ocarina of Time remake. We've only had a glimpse at the game so far - a glimpse that proved controversial for its more realistic art style - and while we've been told it's releasing this year, we don't know when. The suggestion is that the Ocarina of Time remake could launch near or alongside GTA 6 in mid-November, which so far, no other game has dared to do.
We also expect a proper trailer for The Legend of Zelda film - which is due out next year and production is under way on - plus potentially a Switch port or remaster of classic Zelda adventures Wind Waker and Twilight Princess. We may even get the long whispered-about Oracle of Seasons/Ages GBA games in the new-but-retro style of Link's Awakening. Perhaps the legendary SNES game A Link to the Past could be given the same treatment. And dare we hope for a glimpse at the next fully fledged Zelda game?
All of that plus probably some amiibos, maybe a limited edition Zelda-themed Switch 2 design, and a look at the series' history. There's actually quite a lot to be excited about.
Our live coverage of this event has finished.
Good day! Welcome to Nintendo week? What Zelda-related treats would you like to see today? An officially licensed Link fancy dress kit? Zelda hair extensions? A Master Sword kitchen knife?
I dunno if it is just vocal fans or people who really love A-Team-in-the-garage tooks/TotK powers to clip through scenery and stuff, but the contingent wanting a grander 'reimagining' seems greater than I'd have imagined.
I know there's been the Musou game and the Zelda game, but I feel like, in the post OoT period, you had Majora's Mask, you had the GC (/Wii) games and the GBA games, and there was a bit more tolerance for different approaches as a result (a bit more, I say, remembering the Wind Waker graphics complaints). But perhaps that's nothing to do with changes to the Legend of Zelda buffet offer. Perhaps it's just to do with tolerance levels at large.
I would eat up a Link to the Past remake like a piece of forgotten cake at a birthday party.
40 years old. Zelda is basically as old as I am - I have a few years on it. It's funny to think that a series has been alongside someone's life like that. I've dipped in and out of adventures over the years, and still, it's remained. It's still one of the most important series in games. That's quietly quite remarkable, isn't it?
I’d strongly doubt Twilight Princess would drop due to similarity (ie 3D) with OOT.
Four swords! There's a good idea. Ideal for Switch multiplayer as well.
Well, good afternoon again. We're about 10 minutes from the off here. The stream is up and running to some degree - we're seeing a bunch of Switch trailers fill the time.
How many of you have played Splatoon Raiders? I still haven't had a chance. And how many of you were already Splatoon fans?
I'd played a chunk of the mainline games but never had enough time to invest to be truly competitive online. That's not a concern with Raiders!
Oh. Intriguing. I certainly am pumped for the upcoming Fire Emblem. I got very into a 3DS Fire Emblem a bunch of years ago.
Two minutes to go. One minute. We are nearly there. These things tend to go brisky so strap in.
"The presentation will begin soon!" I've always loved Nintendo's enthusiastic exclamation mark. Come on, come on. Let's have you!
And we begin with an orchestral performance of Zelda music as clips of Zelda games gone by flash on teh screen. How many have you played?
I think I jumped in at Zelda 2 on the NES.
Reminds me of that time Miyamoto did a Wii Music performance at E3. But back to Zelda: the on-stage orchestra is growing as we see clips from Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.
Nintendo reminds us how lovely Zelda music is with an orchestral performance
But how recognisable is that music, hey? How many lives has it influenced? The orchestra is full now and the music has roused to a Ganon-themed crescendo. Battle music is playing. Oh, there's a choir now as well!
A classy beginning from Nintendo underlining just how influential and long-running this series is.
Wind Waker! I played that one.
Imagine if you had this music play to wake you up every morning. You'd be as a bright-eyed as Link, wouldn't you?
Shigeru Miyamoto appears on screen to give us a brief rundown of the series, talking about evolutions in technology and experimental controls. All this talk about evolutions: are we going to see a new Zelda game here?
Nope, no. He's saying ghtnak you and goodbye. But not without talking about some new initiatives. And here's the film!
The Legend of Zelda film arrives 30th April
The film is arriving 30th April 2027. The title is simply The Legend of Zelda.
Miyamoto has been helping with the film of course. I wonder what he's like to work with. He's teasing the Triforce's role in the film. Mate, it's the same story every time.
There's lots of Zelda merch coming
Less interesting: there's a special 40th anniversary Zelda exhibition in the Nintendo Museum in Japan. There's also a Link statue in a new family restaurant at the museum, that you still probably can't get to. It's opening this autumn.
But there's a bunch of collectible Zelda stuff coming. An amiibo, some Lego stuff! More! It flashed by very quickly. A playable Ocarina!
New #amiibo figures of Young Link and Young Zelda will be released in 2027. They can be used to unlock special in-game masks in The Legend of #Zelda: Ocarina of Time for Nintendo Switch 2. pic.twitter.com/nYlB2WWXlo
Zelda orchestral concert coming to London in April
The Zelda composer Koji Kondo is on screen talking a bit about the music now. There's a musical anniversary concert coming, but only in Japan, it looks like. Oh! No! It's coming to London in April! 3rd April to be precise.
Nintendo shows Ocarina of Time remake gameplay footage
Zelda overlord Aonuma now and he's talking about Ocarina of Time. Onto the remake and he's talking about it being a faithful reinterpretation. And he's going to show us what he means.
We're seeing actual gameplay footage. We see the slightly plastic-looking Link, with that same slightly chubby art style we glimpsed in teh teaser trailer. The Shire-like Kokiri Forest area looks verdant and inviting.
Link can manually jump this time
This art style will be divisive - it's very cutesy. I wonder how different it looks when Link gets older. Link can now manually jump, so there are some jumping puzzles. An dhe can swim. And swim faster, and dive under the water. Gosh he looks plasticky, like a toy.
Link explores with his little glowing fairy friend Navi. There's a nice haziness about the mossy, stoney, underground interior we're exploring - the tree root interior. And there's the Great Deku Tree, which doesn't look happy.
No loading times, as someone points out, althouth there was a brief one.
The action looks quite snappy. Link is fighting a plant with teeth that looks almost threatening? THere's that edge to it.
The environments look nice and there are some sensible improvements to gameplay, it looks like. There's a chest! We've got the Fairy Slingshot.
You can use the motion controls to fire the slingshot as well as aim with the thumbstick.
It's nice to see actual gameplay - I didn't think we'd get this long a look at the game. But, then, if it's due out this year, you'd hope it was playable by this point.
And as Rahmus points out: I wonder what Link looks like older in the game.
We're going to see another area now.
Hyrule Field is a broad open green place with no apparent textures. Stop it, Bertie! There are textures when Link gets close, but otherwise it's a bit like Breath of the Wild.
There's a new feature called Threads of Time now where you can see your progress through the story and what your next objective is.
If you hold down the A button now, you roll then dash. Dashing is recommended for covering longer distances apparently. Can you imagine!
We've run to the castle gate.
In we go. Hyrule Castle Town looks lovely! A Fable-like, chunky, heaving castle town. Lots of activity, colour and people dancing, for instance.
I love a chunky wooden beam, me.
Link takes a tour around the back alleys showing us the extent of the area, which really us beautiful. Importantly, we're seeing the golden evening sun now, because time moves around you - it doesn't freeze when you're in an area.
Now we're seeing the most important feature in the game: the ocarina.
You can use the Switch mic to hum the Ocarina songs
When you play it, magical things happen. Link just made it morning for some reason - oh because certain events happen at certain times of day. There's a fun feature related to this. you can use the microphone to sing the song!
And you can buy an Ocarina replica from the Nintendo Store. Wait hang on. It actually works in the game? It would, if it recognises pitch via the microphone!
Ocarina remake release date is 5th November
As we can see, not only the graphics have evolved but the gameplay too, Aonuma tells us. It's also now got fully voiced cutscenes.
And now the release date! November 5th.
Reborn through time.The Legend of #Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches November 5th, only on #NintendoSwitch2. pic.twitter.com/OPkxN5NmYe
It's not quite neck and neck with GTA but it's not far off. It seems many of you are quite positive about it too.
There's an Ocarina remake companion app for your phone
There's a companion app coming with the game it looks like, called Notes, I think. It tracks your progress across various activities in the game, and rewards you bonus points for it.
You can also play the ocarina on your smart device, and you can make your own music scores with and share your creations online, which is bonkers, but I sort of love it.
There are quizzes, too, because why not.
A Zelda-themed Switch 2 is on the way
You can transfer rupees from your app to your game, it seems.
Oh, amiibo time. Young Link, Young Zelda, and they unlock special in-game retro looks.
And here's a Zelda-themed Switch 2. It's green and the dock has golden Triforce detail. It's available 29th October. Oh and there's a Pro Controller decal as well.
A The Legend of #Zelda 40th Anniversary-themed #NintendoSwitch2 Pro Controller + display stand and Carrying Case will arrive October 29th. pic.twitter.com/Gw2Kzq68by
We're hearing about the other Zelda games we can currently play on Switch, but I don't think there are any announcements related to this.
Oh, and that's everything! They're going to conclude with another trailer for the Ocarina of Time remake.
The show closes with another long look at the Ocarina remake
Here's adult Link riding around on his horsey, and he looks a bit less plasticky strange. We're seeing various different areas now, including deserty ones. Underground temples, swimming. Flying chickens. Fishing. Diving. Um, waterskiing?
It's strange hearing voices in Ocarina of Time. And there's a very sweaty-looking Ganon.
It's a decent trailer - there's a lot in it. Is that Matt Mercer again as Ganon?
A full-on remake, for sure.
A surprisingly focused showing from Nintendo today but I don't know if I mind that? I liked that brazenness of just focusing on Ocarina gameplay and giving us a proper look at it. I suppose I'm disappointed not to see more of Zelda and to hear what's coming next but we've got to leave something for another Nintendo Direct, I guess.
The first print run of the Ocarina of Time remake will have special packaging
Additional information about the Ocarina of Time remake via a press release says that it will have: "completely overhauled visuals, fully voiced cutscenes, expanded character dialogue, symphonic orchestral music, reworked camera and movement controls and more".
"Link's milestone 1998 adventure has been reborn for a whole new era. The first print run of the physical version will commemorate the release with special packaging that features textured foil cover art, available while supplies last."
The first print run of the physical version of The Legend of #Zelda: #OcarinaOfTime for Nintendo Switch 2 will feature special textured foil packaging while supplies last. pic.twitter.com/o8SNZEBa2M
There are going to be two ocarinas on sale
Nintendo's press gumpf clarifies that there are going to be two ocarinas that go on sale: "a playable version for the musically inclined and an electric version from HORI that plays notes or entire songs at the press of a button".
There's no word on price or availability yet.
Information and presumably tickets for the Zelda orchestral performances apparently open on zelda.gameconcerts.com later today, but that website is currently password protected for me.
There's a bit more information on the smartphone-linked Zelda Notes app. This is apparently already avaiable for use with Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.
"Support for The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will help players track their adventure, challenge them to find in-game locations using hint images, let them play a virtual ocarina, take a daily quiz with over 2,000 total questions and more."
An Ocarina Lego set is on the way, and a replica Master Sword
A press release has also revealed that there's a 1750-piece Link and Epona Lego Set on the way "for adults" starting spring 2027.
And Hasbro is apparently making a 27-inch electronic Master Sword with motion-activated sounds to be avilable from spring 2027 as well. Presumably it's also for adults? It doesn't say.
Incidentally, if you're only just joining us, we've got a handy Everything announced in today's Nintendo Zelda Direct article to catch you up, if you don't fancy scrolling down here.
A Japanese website for the Ocarina of Time remake has gone live, by the way, with some more imagery on it.
Nintendo said there was "a lot of discussion" about Ocarina remake look
There is also now a text version of the video we watched earlier, so we can see more easily what each Nintendo person said.
When talking about the Ocarina of Time, Eiji Aonuma, boss of the Zelda series, said: "We had a lot of discussion about what the visuals for this game should look like. We wanted to create something completely new, but at the same time, we wanted Link to be a vibrant character living in a world that feels somewhat nostalgic. That's how we arrived at this design.
"The clothes and equipment have also been completely redesigned, and I think you'll be able to feel the texture of the materials, but we didn't just aim for a realistic representation; we focused on 'reimagining the essence of Ocarina of Time in a way that evokes a sense of nostalgia'."
Aonuma also picked on points such as there being no freely controllable camera in Ocarina the first time around, because the game only had one joystick. This is particularly noticeable in a place like Hyrule Castle Town where the camera is no longer fixed. You can play mini-games there, apparently, and Nintendo has added "quite a bit of dialogue to characters in this game to bring out their personalities even more".
When remarking on the game's performance, Aonuma said "the processing speed is much faster in this game compared to the N64 era, so the action moves smoothly and responsively". I mean, you'd hope it would, given that it's been nearly 30 years since the original came out.
"As you've seen, the graphics have evolved significantly, of course, but the ease of play has also improved dramatically, resulting in a brand new Ocarina of Time."
That's it for our rolling coverage for the day. We'll be back tomorrow for another more generalised Nintendo Direct, don't forget. Join us again then. That's an order. And thanks for joining us today!
Tune in tomorrow, September 9th at 15:00 (UK time) for #NintendoDirect. The livestreamed presentation will feature around 45 minutes of info on #NintendoSwitch2 games launching this winter.Watch here: https://t.co/JsqVG5hqm3 pic.twitter.com/NVOQc2QGfc
We're a day later and perhaps you don't care at this point but there's a nice video here comparing the original Ocarina with the remake. The notable difference to me, barring the graphical changes, is the frame-rate. It's much smoother now.
There's also some concern that the Zelda-themed Switch 2 is a Japan-only thing. Nintendo seems to suggest as much on its official website.

News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 11:12 a.m. 49 comments Follow Grand Theft Auto VI Prioritise us on Google Grand Theft Auto 6 arrives 19th November on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S. Depending on where you may be in the world, however, when you actually get to play varies.
Starting with PS5, GTA 6 has 15 different regional launch times. If you pre-ordered a digital copy through the PlayStation Store, the game's unlock time will be dictated by your account's region and store. In other words, it won't unlock for everyone at the same time.
GTA fansite GTAVice.net rifled through PlayStation Store data to uncover the full list of launch times across its 15 regions. The unlock times range between 11am UTC on 18th November at the earliest, to 6am UTC on 19th November - a 19-hour difference.
As is common with staggered releases, New Zealand goes first. GTA 6 becomes playable there at 12am NZDT on 19th November (midnight on 18th November). Mexico, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua are the last to gain access, where the game unlocks at 12am CST on 20th November (midnight on 19th November).
Notably, the release timestamps don't appear on the PlayStation Store pages for every country with a PS Store page. GTAVice lists Bahrain, China, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman and Qatar as all missing that information. For countries like The Philippines, Russia, Serbia and Vietnam their store pages instead redirect you to other countries' stores.
It's worth reiterating that your unlock time is tied to the PlayStation Store's account region, not where you physically are in the world. For instance, if you reside in Canada but made your digital pre-order on the UK store, the game will unlock for you when it does for everyone in the UK.
We actually got reminded of that regional split shortly after pre-orders went live for the code-in-box "physical" version of the game, as multiple retailers issued warnings that codes are region-locked. Rockstar later clarified which countries are affected, and which codes can only be redeemed in the country they were bought.
Things are more interesting on Xbox, however, as the console platform allows users to switch regions and stores through the system menu, meaning copies aren't locked to any particular region. As anyone who's done that trick to play Call of Duty games early each year knows, of course, changing your region to New Zealand is all you need to play GTA 6 as soon as humanly possible.

Image credit: IWGB News by Robert Purchese Associate Editor Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 10:24 a.m. 34 comments Follow Grand Theft Auto VI Prioritise us on Google Two weeks after Grand Theft Auto 6's Netflix reveal, and only a couple of months before the game's meteoric release, Rockstar Games has an employment tribunal to fight. This week, the final hearing in Rockstar vs. the 31 fired Rockstar North employees begins.
Here, Rockstar has to finally face the allegations it "unlawfully" fired those 31 employees and "blacklisted" them for being a part of a union - allegations levelled at it by the union the employees belonged to: the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Rockstar tried to have these claims thrown out earlier this year but the employment tribunal ruled against it.
The final hearing is a long process. It begins Thursday, 10th September but runs through to 16th October - just over a month before GTA 6 arrives. The IWGB seeks, on the workers' behalf, either reinstatement or compensation, "as well as a finding from the tribunal that their dismissals were unfair", the IWGB said in a press release.
"For almost a year, the truth about what happened to us has been buried by Rockstar and surrounded by speculation. Now we finally get the chance to put it on the record," said former Rockstar employee Jason Lewis. "None of us imagined that talking to each other about our working conditions would turn our lives upside down and catapult us into the centre of a global media storm.
"As the world prepares for the release of GTA 6, we are reliving the heartbreak of being thrown out of a project we poured so much of our lives into. We lost our jobs, our income, our community and the chance to see the game through to release after spending years helping to build it. It was devastating.
"We have fought tooth and nail to get to this point, not just to be able to win justice for ourselves, but to draw a line in the sand for any employer that thinks it can attack workers for unionising. It has been an emotional journey and it is not over yet, but we can now see the finish line, and justice at last feels within reach."
Rockstar fired 34 employees in October last year - 31 of those employees at Rockstar North in Scotland - for what it alleged was "gross misconduct". Rockstar said the employees were breaching confidentiality agreements by talking about the company in a private IWGB Discord channel. But the employees - speaking to our friends at People Make Games, who have covered and continue to cover this topic extensively - maintain they were discussing salaries and HR issues related to employment. The sorts of things that would be discussed in a union-related Discord channel.
These 31 Rockstar North employees were fired with immediate effect and escorted from the building. One Australian employee was reportedly forced to return to Australia after Rockstar withdrew his work visa and reported him to the Home Office, the IWGB claimed. This all resulted in widespread media coverage and protests, resulting in the matter being raised in UK Parliament and being commented upon by then Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
"It's a deeply concerning case," Starmer said. "Every worker has the right to join a trade union and we're determined to strengthen workers rights and ensure they don't face unfair consequences for being part of a union."
Ahead of this week's final tribunal hearing, IWGB president Alex Marshall said: "We believe Rockstar has tried to get away with Grand Theft Employment Rights. After a year of fighting to get answers, we hope this tribunal will finally back them into a corner and bring the truth to light."
This is not the first time Rockstar or its parent company Take-Two has taken issue with Discord. Indeed, Take-Two is currently legally trying to force private user information out of Discord relating to the recent leaks of GTA 6 gameplay footage.
As a result of the union-related firings, a Rockstar Game Workers Union has sprung up and continues to grow in size. The Rockstar Game Workers Union has made several other allegations against the company relating to enforcing crunch, weaponising bonus payments, and failing to address gender-based pay inequality.

Image credit: Nintendo News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 9:24 a.m. 26 comments Prioritise us on Google The updated Nintendo Switch 2 model has started shipping, and players are taking it apart to see how it differs from the launch model. In case you're unaware, Nintendo announced it's developing new revisions of the Switch 2 console and its accessories that comply with the European Union's Right to Repair directive and updated battery regulations.
In order to comply with the EU's rules, battery-powered devices must allow users to easily access and replace their batteries. Nintendo previously said the new model would became available starting sometime this summer, and now the revised design has started hitting store shelves.
In a video comparing the launch model with the EU-compliant revision, YouTube channel Nintendúo opens up both units to show all the differences. As Nintendo's updated designs revealed in July, the new model does indeed have a smaller battery. Battery capacity has been cut down by 1 percent, or about 48 mAh. The console - with Joy-Cons attached - is also 14 grams heavier.
One of the most immediately recognisable changes is how visible the screws inside the Joy-Con rails are, which previously were hidden under warranty void / anti-tamper stickers. This is what makes accessing the console's insides much more straightforward.
After popping the back cover off, we can see the heat shield no longer extends to cover the battery, making it easier to access and replace. To protect against heat, the battery is now wrapped in thick insulation.
The two models are difficult to tell apart without physically holding the box. If you're able to zoom in on the product page online, look for visible screws in the Joy-Con rails. The updated model also bears the OSM product code, with the serial number beginning with HLE in Europe.
The Joy-Cons and Switch 2 Pro Controller are all getting revisions at various times throughout the year, with the N64 and GameCube controllers instead getting updated in early 2027. The video does not show teardowns for any of the controllers. Nintendo is also planning on selling replaceable batteries alongside a kit that includes detailed steps on how to access, remove and replace the battery.
Nintendo is replacing Switch 2 models across retailers on a rolling basis, meaning you can't pick which revision to purchase - without looking closely, as detailed in this story.

An Indian fighter and framed policeman on the run, he'll be coming to the popular fighting game next month.
This trailer, which you can watch below, follows the norm established by prior SF6 trailers by going through each of his normal and special moves, before delving into fancy looking combos and supers. Aside from being a bulky brawler, Arjun has power over both wind and earth, using both elements to his advantage.

News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 8, 2026, 8:11 a.m. 8 comments Follow Forza Horizon 6 Prioritise us on Google Forza Horizon 6 developer Playground Games has shot down rumours the game's anticipated PlayStation 5 version had been delayed. The confirmation, slim as it is, comes a little over one week after reports about a quiet delay for Horizon 6 started surfacing.
In a blog post covering Forza Horizon 6's latest major update, Playground reaffirmed the open-world driving game is coming to PS5 this year, though without announcing a solid release date or suggesting a release window.
"If you're planning your trip to Discover Japan on PlayStation 5, stay tuned! Forza Horizon 6 will be releasing on PS5 later this year, and you can add the game to your wishlist on the PlayStation Store to be notified of availability," reads a paragraph tucked away near the end of the post.
This was certainly surprising to see, as even before last week's reports, players just assumed the game had quietly slipped out of 2026 simply because the developer stopped talking about it. Horizon 6 was revealed during 2025's Tokyo Game Show, almost exactly one year ago. It made sense, given the game's Japan setting, so it would likewise make sense for Xbox to return to the TGS stage to announce a PS5 release date. TGS 2026 takes place 17th-21st September, so we won't have to wait too long to get our answer.

Image credit: Eurogamer News by Kaan Serin Contributor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 7:05 p.m. 17 comments Follow Persona 2: Eternal Punishment Prioritise us on Google With Persona 3 Reload out the door and Persona 4 Revival next in line, series producer Kazuhisa Wada has said remakes of the first two games will "probably" happen as well.
Developer Atlus seems to be on a mission to revisit every high-schooling, demon-mashing, double-life-simulating game it's ever made. In 2024, the studio pulled the gun on Persona 3 Reload before starting work on Persona 4 Revival, coming next February. But Atlus may reach even further back for some new (old) source material.
In an interview with RPS, Wada said the team originally came up with the idea to remake Persona 3 and Persona 4 around the same time. The latter "had to be put" on the backburner for a while, but the intent for both was the same. "I think a remaster or remake is some kind of cultural preservation," he said, per a translator.
Wada continued to explain that it's Atlus' "duty" to make sure its older games aren't lost to time "and are still around in the modern day." With that in mind, "Persona 1 and 2 are something we'll probably eventually do, too." There you have it, folks.
Persona 1 and Persona 2 are also the only mainline games in the series that aren't readily available to buy on any modern system, making Wada's point about "cultural preservation" even more salient here.
Regardless, I think it always made sense to begin this remake voyage with Persona 3, the game that spawned the series' more recognisable features (social elements, dating, etc) and notably didn't include a major antagonist that might be tricky to depict in the same way nowadays (a rumour-fuelled Hitler reincarnation).
A few years back, a prominent Sega leaker claimed that Persona 1 and 2 remakes were in the works, alongside a Persona 4 remake that hadn't been made official at the time. It wasn't clear how substantially different those rumoured remakes would be, however.

I'm talking about Ariana Grande, of course.
For those not in the know, Final Fantasy Resonance is an almost unrecognisable reconstruction of the now-shuttered mobile game Final Fantasy Brave Exvius. It's not exactly a port or a remake, but it's using the original game's story as a jumping off point.
And one of Final Fantasy Resonance's most unique ideas comes from Visions, characters from across the series' history who you can summon in battle. Cloud and Lightning and Cecil can all lend you a helping hand while in combat, but modders have now taken things a step further by adding every Brave Exvius fighter who didn't make it onto Resonance's roster.
The FFR Vision Studio mod brings almost 1,300 Brave Exvius units into the upcoming game's demo as Visions. That means every guest character from the defunct mobile game can theoretically show up, Kingdom Hearts' Sora and Nier Automata's 2B included.
Brave Exvius caught a lot of flack many years ago because, well, the game wasn't exactly good. Seemingly nonsensical guest characters, like Ariana Grande and Katy Perry, also rubbed fans the wrong way, though the more gay and chronically online members of the fanbase (me) have since warmed up to how silly and sometimes camp those crossovers were.
Speaking to Kotaku, producer Keisuke Nakashima explained that "Ariana Grande's character would not fit within the vibe that we've created for Final Fantasy Resonance." It all depends on your perspective, Nakashima.
A recent blog post and an accompanying roadmap show that there's still work left to be done on the mod. The modder in charge said they're working on making the animations better and adding in a skill dictionary for the Brave Exvius abilities, and they might even develop side quests to dish out certain Visions.

Image credit: Eurogamer/Firaxis News by Matt Wales Staff Writer Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 5:31 p.m. 11 comments Follow Sid Meier's Civilization VII Prioritise us on Google It's been a bumpy ride for Civilization 7, but two years after its widely criticised launch - and as the legendary 4X series celebrates its 35th anniversary - developer Firaxis has unveiled a host of new updates coming to the game. That includes an atomic age update, dragging Civ 7 into the present and beyond, as well as its first paid expansion, Earthrise, both arriving next year.
Starting with the free Arc of Tomorrow update, it finally drags Civ 7's current end-game into more contemporary times. It introduces a new age, the Atomic Age, extending the current playable timeline from the 1950s into the near future, and adds period-specific gameplay, alongside new buildings, units, visuals, and more. As with other Ages, it'll be possible to begin a game straight from in the Atomic Age, or go the long way round, starting in Antiquity.
As to what the Atomic Age brings, there're new civilisations and leaders, as well as expanded nuclear gameplay options, including "a fun twist on mutually assured destruction." New Multilateral Agreements enable leaders to "collectively react to developing situations - like a growing stockpile of nuclear warheads - with calls for disarmament or escalation", and new empire management tools provide options such as the ability to transform Settlements into new City-States. Among other things, City-States enable Proxy Warfare focused on smaller-scale conflicts rather than all-out empire warfare.
"There's a compelling need to honour the uncertainty and fear present in [the recent past], where proxy warfare became the new norm by which global conflict was conducted and the spectre of nuclear war loomed, as it still does today," Firaxis writes. "But there were also moments of light, triumph, and hope. Things once thought impossible, like spaceflight, were challenged and overcome as technology advanced at a rapid pace, while marginalised peoples rallied together to fight for justice and equality."
Elsewhere in Arc of Tomorrow, it'll be possible to make Great Works of Film that gives different benefits depending on the quality of the movie produced. These require Film Crews to hunt for the perfect filming location, which changes depending on your desired genre. Additionally, the introduction of Manufactured Goods means players can combine specific commodities to create powerful new resources like Enriched Uranium. Playtesting for Arc of Tomorrow begins this year, and sign up details are here.
Once Civilization 7 has been yanked into the modern age, Firaxis is pushing even further into the future with the launch of the game's space-race-themed first paid expansion. "From humanity's earliest days, we have always been fascinated with the sky," it writes. "In Earthrise, that sense of wonder shapes your civilisation's story from the Antiquity Age all the way to the near future."
Details on Earthrise are currently limited, but Firaxis says it's currently 'envisioning' space-themed gameplay mechanics that unlock new bonuses in each Age. During the Antiquity and Exploration Ages, for instance, you might chart the night sky and name the celestial bodies to gain insights about the solar system, and you might launch early orbital missions around Earth and the moon in the Modern Age. As for the Atomic Age, expect to establish your own space agency and launch missions to the stars, uncovering planetary features and resources you can exploit back on Earth.
Earthrise also includes a focus on environmental adaptability, such as the ability for players to alter the terrain and their empire's tile bonuses, and to gain biome bonuses as they become more proficient at working the land in each biome. Additionally, there's talk of new civil engineering structures to fight back against rising global temperatures and increasing Natural Disasters - including the ability to reverse the warming itself.
Arc of Tomorrow and Earthrise (Civ 7's first paid expansion, but not its first paid DLC - there've been strong complaints from the community about the fact it already has over £100 of DLC) are both planned for release in 2027, with Arc of Tomorrow coming first. Before all that, however, there's Civilization 7's new 1.5.0 update, which is coming later this month. It includes the True Start Location Earth map, new Terra Incognita and Shuffle Voronoi maps, plus updates to diplomacy, resource generation, and UI.

Image credit: Panache Digital News by Robert Purchese Associate Editor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 4:12 p.m. 8 comments Follow 1666: Amsterdam Prioritise us on Google Patrice Désilets, the creator of the Assassin's Creed series and director of 1666: Amsterdam, has said he will make a sequel to open-world human evolution survival game Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey.
Désilets, talking to me at a recent 1666: Amsterdam event, said 2019's Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey was written as a "volume one". "I've designed different volumes to eventually be growing the game," he said.
I didn't think he owned the Ancestors franchise - I thought Take-Two's sold-off publishing label Private Division did. However, Désilets replied: "I own the IP. But it's complex."
So he could make a sequel if he wanted to. "Yeah," he confirmed. "I will. I will. And people can believe me because I'm ready to wait 16 fucking years to finish what I started [with 1666 Amsterdam]; I finish what I started."
Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey was an imaginative concept, a game that charted humankind's evolution from primate into upright walking human, across millions of years of time. As a player, you survived through different eras of third-person action survival gameplay, as the game lurched millions of years through time.
We liked the idea though not so much the execution. "Ancestors is ambitious and clunky and not much fun," wrote Donlan in his Ancestors: The Humankind Odyssey Eurogamer review, "and it's often quietly thought-provoking too." But despite its clunkiness, Ancestors managed to find a sizeable audience, selling 2m copies as of April 2024.
However, Ancestors was really a stepping-stone to Désilets' long-held ambition to make a dark Amsterdam-based open-world adventure in 1666: Amsterdam. The idea had been knocking around for a long time but was redesigned in COVID lockdown and entered production shortly after.
And again, 1666: Amsterdam is imaginative, but again, the execution is uneven, as Donlan elaborated on in his 1666: Amsterdam early access review. There is also a side of gen-AI-helped controversy to be aware of.
Crucially, 1666: Amsterdam is not finished yet. This is an early access release and there's "less than half" in the game of what Désilets wants. The Steam page for 1666: Amsterdam estimates early access will take "approximately a year", but also: "It is difficult to accurately predict precisely how long early access will last."
To me, Désilets said: "The toughest part is done. Now it's all about production and making - we would say 'the poutine'." It took several years to get to this point, but now the groundwork is laid. "Now it's all about 'let's make pizzas'," he said, by way of a reference.
More importantly: "We have a plan," he said. "That's important. We have a plan. We have stuff we want to make, there's space for comeback from the community in the plan, but it could go on forever at the same time. That's not the main plan; you'll have a 1.0 version."
It's also worth noting that 1666: Amsterdam currently sits at a "mixed" reception on Steam with only 720 reviews, suggesting it hasn't found a large or very receptive audience yet. Whatever Ancestors sequel there may be, then, not only has to wait until this game is finished, but may also depend on if it succeeds.

According to new analysis, the PC storefront has made $15bn (~£11.10bn) already this year, representing Valve's cut from selling games, DLC and software on its platform.
So what was Steam's biggest revenue-generating new game release? That would be Forza Horizon 6, based on new Alinea Analytics data. The firm's analysis shows the open-world racing game has generated an estimated $210.5m (~£155.74m) in revenue for Valve.
Horizon 6 is followed closely by another major 2026 hit, Crimson Desert, itself having brought Valve $203.3m (~£150.42m) in revenue. Rounding out to the top three is Resident Evil Requiem, which made Valve $200.9m (~£148.64m) in revenue.
According to Alinea analyst Rhys Elliott, the top six highest-grossing new releases on Steam only amounted to just $1bn (~£735.8m) of that $15bn, or just 6.6 percent. Incidentally, two games in the top six - Crimson Desert and Meccha Chameleon - come from new intellectual properties (IPs).
Expanding the scope further to include the top 100 highest-grossing new releases in 2026, we see the value grows to $2.4bn (~£1.78bn) or a more respectable 15.9 percent of the store's overall revenue so far.
The data is skewed a little, however, as Crimson Desert is responsible for 18 percent ($203m) of the new IP revenue of that because of how successful it was. Take Crimson Desert out, and that 63 percent drops to just 39 percent.
There are plenty of upcoming, highly-anticipated releases yet left in 2026, however. Just last week we saw the release of two hits in Onimusha: Way of the Sword and The Blood of Dawnwalker. There was suspicion of this last week, ahead of DLSS 5's debut implementation in NBA 2K27, and now it's been properly tested, the performance toll has been confirmed. The experts at Digital Foundry declared it "super, super heavy".
Digital Foundry highlighted an approximately 40-60 percent frame-rate difference in NBA 2K27 when DLSS 5 was turned on. A topline GeForce RTX 5090 card running the game in Ultra settings at native 4K resolution dropped from 128.4 FPS to 62.7 FPS, for example. Even an RTX 5060 running Ultra settings in 1080p dropped from 72.8 FPS to 42.3 FPS.
"This is super, super heavy," Digital Foundry founder Richard Leadbetter said, "but it's also running on the entire RTX 50 series stack including laptops, which I didn't anticipate." And he added: "That's couched by the fact that, compared to a triple-A colossus, this is a relatively light game by comparison, so that has an impact."
The primary point of performance discussion was around "frame-time cost", which is a relatively fixed cost with DLSS 5, apparently. This varies from 8.2ms to 13.7ms depending on the graphics card and resolution being used. "Eight milliseconds of processing time at 4K on a 5090: that's mega expensive," Leadbetter said, "let's put it this way."
DLSS 5 was criticised ferociously in March when it was announced for using a gen-AI-powered "neural rendering" to alter the appearance of characters in games. Digital Foundry's John Linneman was particularly outspoken against this aspect of it, so it's interesting to see him be impressed by NBA 2K27's "very, very subtle" implementation here.
"It actually works pretty well, I would say," Linneman said, highlighting the effect DLSS 5 has on crowd lighting and on a player's jersey, adding a kind of drop-shadow depth which wouldn't be there otherwise. And that's it; there's no character textural alteration.
"I felt like this was pushing back against what we saw in March," Linneman added, "which was just wholesale, massive changes to the way games were looking, to the point where it almost felt like you had lights being added from places where logically there would be no light and stuff like that. And I didn't really feel like that with NBA, so it was a convincing example."
But, as he later pointed out, "It just seems like a really expensive way to add nice lighting detail into the image," even if "it doesn't seem as crazy as it first sounded".
The Digital Foundry video showed footage of NBA 2K27 running with DLSS 5 on, as well as glimpses of the tech modded into games like Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth, Monster Hunter Rise, and Starfield. The team's general thoughts were this was a first attempt at a technology that will likely improve in time, which tallies with Nvidia's pledge to keep improving performance, though there's obviously concern about how it will develop from here.
It's a confusing prospect for DLSS, which has until now been a technology that's improved performance in games by lowering the native resolution and then upscaling the image. This DLSS 5 development is the first time it's attempted something otherwise, and perhaps this signals the future for it going forwards. DLSS 5 is currently only available for 50-series GeForce cards and only officially in NBA 2K27.

Image credit: Blizzard News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 12:19 p.m. 9 comments Follow StarCraft Prioritise us on Google The rumblings about the next StarCraft game continue to get louder. Following recent reports that Korean developer-publisher Nexon had acquired the rights to develop a sequel in the sci-fi franchise, the official StarCraft 2 website started displaying visual glitches, clearly signaling some sort of impending announcement.
Now, thanks to new information, we may have some idea of what kind of game it's going to be. According to Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier, we should rule out the possibility of the next StarCraft game being a Destiny-style live service shooter.
Schreier revealed this tidbit in a recent chat with former Polygon guides producer Ryan Gilliam, though without saying more besides. "I wouldn't count on this StarCraft game being a Destiny-like, I'll say that," said Schreier.
This was a particularly disappointing revelation for the host, who wanted another well-funded studio to carry Destiny's mantle. It is also notable that Blizzard, a developer of several mega-successful live service games, seemingly isn't making one in this instance - at least, from what we're working with here.
So if not Destiny-like, what recent game can the StarCraft project be compared to? Well, according to Windows Central editor Jez Corden, it may be a Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2-like and seemingly even takes cues from the Far Cry series.
"From what I saw it's more Space Marine 2 / Far Cry kinda adjacent, but dunno for sure what the overall gameplay formula will be," Corden wrote on X.
The Far Cry name drop is curious, as it's long been reported that former Far Cry boss Dan Hay is helming a StarCraft shooter at Blizzard. Space Marine 2 and Far Cry don't share many similarities, so it's unclear exactly what features Corden is referring to there.
Whatever Blizzard has in store for us will be demystified this weekend at BlizzCon. The show takes place 12th-13th September, and given recent teases, the opening ceremony is everyone's best guess as to when the game will be unveiled.

Image credit: Panache Digital Games Review by Christian Donlan Contributing Editor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 12:01 p.m. 22 comments Follow 1666: Amsterdam Prioritise us on Google There's an old Sam Raimi profile in the New Yorker I think about quite a bit. This is because, mid-way through the piece, Raimi says one of the most interesting things I've ever heard a film-maker, or any kind of creative person, put into words.
Raimi's talking about the films he made with his friends when they were really young. Super-8 stuff. The camera would swoop in on two toy soldiers stood up on the carpet, and then the film would cut to Sam and a friend standing next to each other. And this is the thing: nobody watching the film would understand what the two shots cut together were meant to represent. They were telling you that Sam and his friend were the soldiers on the carpet. That's what you were meant to take away. But everybody in the audience missed it.
Raimi then explains - and I wish I had the quote - that as a kid he was making films that were so bad that nobody could even tell they were bad. The audience was just bemused. For the audience to understand that they were watching a bad film, Raimi would first have to become a better film-maker.
I appreciate this sounds like a brutal way to open a discussion of a video game, but be warned: if anything, I suspect I like 1666: Amsterdam a lot more than most people will. Even so, there's no ducking the fact that it is an odd game. And it's often odd through necessity, I imagine.
And this is why I thought of Raimi. In one sequence early on in the game - no matter why any of this was happening - I was wandering through a 1990s boutique hotel in Amsterdam almost entirely naked. I was trying to get to an outside space that I had just seen in a vision. But my path was blocked, and it was blocked by strange, low-res groupings of people, their faces not much more than bland cartoons. They were standing together, perfectly still if my memory is correct, clustered in doorways. What to make of it all? These groupings, so almost-sketched in, each one with at least one entirely replicated person amongst their number. And so still! So blank of expression. I had no idea what to think. Was this a dream? Were these people possessed? Had we fallen outside of time and space somehow?
What I now reckon is this: the game needed to hem me in, to drive me towards tackling a specific puzzle about getting to that outdoor space. And it wanted me to tackle that specific puzzle in a specific way. So it used crowds to close out doors I wasn't meant to go through. But because of the challenges of making an ambitious game with a relatively small team and a limited budget, it had to rely on low-res character models. And it had to duplicate some of them. And I don't think it could animate them at this specific point. That's my guess.
This led to Raimi-style confusion. Forget good or bad, what even is this? What am I meant to take from this moment? But untangling this whole sequence also led me to understanding something about 1666: Amsterdam. I'm on its side. It's not bad. In fact, some of it is really good in principle. But in trying to execute on an ambitious plan, the whole thing's over-stretched itself. And hence a game about witchcraft contains accidental surrealism along with the real thing.
This is the pact you make with 1666: Amsterdam, I think. To enjoy it you have to survive a bunch of things that are not really that enjoyable. There's the AI stuff in the game, of course, which is just as miserable as always. Then there are the bugs and rough edges. Alongside the odd crash, I've had to quit and restart numerous times because the cat I was playing as - I'll get to this - descended into the game's geometry and got stuck. Walking through Amsterdam's busy streets, the people I pass are animated, but they're still regularly duplicated, a city of twins and triplets. And I cannot work out the rules governing who has collision turned off (most people) and who doesn't (some people, some times).
A lot of voices online are saying that the game's in too rough a shape to be heading to early access like this. And I guess that's true. But I guess what's also true is that, again, a fairly small team is making this game, and the design is complex and at times pretty audacious. Sometimes, I imagine you need to get money coming in just so that you can keep on trucking. There you are: another kind of pact.
Anyway. As I write this I'm still in the early sections of 1666: Amsterdam's current early access build. I'm told there's about 15 hours in it total, and I'm just nearing the end of the first proper mission. I'm about six hours in. The reason I've stopped playing now to write this is because I've hit a bit of a milestone. I've just beaten a boss, sure, and I'm about to get to the outer arm of what I assume the main loop is. But more than that, after being intrigued and frustrated and confused by what I've been playing, I've finally hit on what feels like the peculiar magic of this game. I've found the thing that makes it worth playing and that actually makes it kind of wonderful.
1666: Amsterdam is a tale of witchcraft and devilry, and it's made by Patrice Désilets' team at Panache. Panache made the memorably odd and frustrating and thought-provoking Ancestors, in which you guide an early hominid through the wonky chicanes of evolution. But Désilets himself is probably best known for his work on Assassin's Creed.
And 1666: Amsterdam initially looks a lot like Assassin's Creed. This is potentially a problem, because that's a really bad lens through which to view this game. But again, you play someone in the present who's learning about someone in the past. You dance between time periods - three in this game: the present day, the 1990s, and the year 1666. In the 1666 part you play someone in a hood that hides all but the surly curl of their lip, and that person is tasked with tracking down various targets in the city and getting rid of them. That sure sounds like Assassin's Creed!
But in fact things are very different. I'm going to focus on the 1666 part here because, from what I can tell, it's both the main event and the most satisfying part. Noa, who you play as in this era, is a kind of assassin, perhaps, but she's primarily a witch. And while she can gad about the waterways when nobody's looking, and engage in staff-based combat when she really has to, she can't mantle and wall-run like Ezio and all the rest of them. For the most part she has to keep her witch self concealed and move about Amsterdam meekly, avoiding any kind of scrutiny.
So rather than scaling towers and dropping out of the sky to put a blade through someone's throat, she wanders the streets and listens to crowd chatter and slowly works out the identity of her next witchy target. In the first proper mission, this is a prosecutor of some kind who is known for being particularly tough on witches. With her perp IDd, Noa then needs to gather a bunch of evidence before the prosecutor can be unmasked and dispatched - cue boss fight.
Real talk: I am not enjoying combat in this game. With its jumps and flourishes it looks wonderful, but Noa is too delicate - a few hits and she's gone - and her dash move is too useful for creating space. Together, these things mean that I avoid the more complicated options I have, which involve special attacks and witch-based triggering of environmental hazards, and I just lamp people with my wooden stick and then dash out of harm's way. It gets me through most battles without too much annoyance, but it is the opposite of fun. For me, I think the diagnosis is this: failing is so arduous that I just want to work through the fights as conservatively as I can. In other words, the balance is off.
But the stuff in between that? This is the part of the game I think I may love. And this really is an inversion of Assassin's Creed. Rather than a huge city to scramble over the outside of, 1666: Amsterdam gives you a single neighborhood of Amsterdam at any one time, but it seems to model the insides as well as the outsides of most buildings. It's practically an immersive sim, albeit one that feels like it's arrived at that genre unintentionally. This is that rare open world game where you can actually step through most doors and see what's lying beyond them. All of this is delivered with wonderful lighting that invokes the spooky art of the Dutch Golden Age.
This sounds overwhelming: a whole neighborhood to explore. In truth, the game's pretty quick to put you onto the correct target. Within minutes of leaving the house to uncover my foe, I had been directed towards a trial taking place and I was pretty sure I had my man.
Now I had to prove it, though. And that meant finding out where this prosecutor lived and then infiltrating their house to look for the things I needed to prove their demonic guilt. And so I discovered that a lot of 1666: Amsterdam is about sneaking through someone's private residence and trying to open as many of its locked doors as you can.
The house I wanted into was both extremely large, being spread over several floors, and heavily patrolled by guards. Going in there as Noa was not an option. Instead, I could use my witch's cat. This cat is where the game's parkour-like elements come in. It can climb up gutters and jump between ledges. And because it's a cat in a city filled with rats and other vermin, it can pretty much go wherever it wants. Pretty soon I had got the cat into the house I was targeting and I was casing the joint, threading through guards' feet, locating the kitchen, the dining room, various bedrooms.
But vital rooms were still locked off. And at this point the game really becomes a spatial puzzle. Over time I realised I could leave the house via an upstairs window and move around the outside ledges a little to access some of the locked rooms, at which point my cat could unlock doors from the inside. Neat trick.
Even neater, I could possess specific guards - any that were visibly scared by the presence of a cat - and then use them to walk about the building and access new parts of it. Certain possessed guards could club other guards and get them out of the way. And one of them, I found, could actually invite Noa inside, taking me along with me, as it were, and then Noa could explore spaces and root through drawers and get the evidence she (I?) needed.
Now. This is very complex, and it's also a bit silly. A lot of big moments in the game are signalled by a stately Dutch person having a massive scrap with a cat. But what I like about all this is not just that it's a bunch of lovely illicit spatial challenges - who doesn't like nosing through other people's things in a game? What I like is that it seems to get at an interesting truth about the era that the game examines.
I'm not an expert on the art of the Dutch Golden Age, but I am a fan. And even if you're a very lapsed fan, you'll experience this game as a bunch of pleasant little instances of shocked recognition. The game opens with a collection of still lives, the paintings of everyday objects and fruits and vegetables that a master like Adriaen Coorte could really make sing. His bunches of asparagus look as vast and godly as alien space ships. His apples and pears look like dwarf planets floating undiscovered in the Kuiper Belt.
And then you're in Amsterdam itself. The complex windows. The red brick. The little arches and doorways. You only need to see a handful of Vermeers or Rembrandts to know how lovingly this stuff has been observed. I walked 1666: Amsterdam and I was in a permanent flashback for a life I had never lived, but had only experienced through oil paintings.
But here's the thing. My limited understanding of one of the real breakthroughs of Dutch art is that this prosperous country - prosperous for some deeply awful reasons, obviously - was one of the first to really turn art inwards. People like Vermeer stayed in their houses for the most part and just painted what they found there.
These are great artists of material culture, and they spoke to a time of merchants and traders. They spoke to a time where your home and its contents were clues to the puzzle of who you truly were - or who you wanted to present yourself as, at the very least. (This goes back a few centuries to van Eyck, incidentally. And van Eyck, to use a bit of art history jargon, is the absolute freakin' business. When the zombie apocalypse finally comes, you'll find me in the National Gallery trying to ease his Arnolfini Portrait out of an open window.)
Marry this art to a game about poking through other peoples' houses and there's something there that I think is really harmonious. And there is something about Panache, too. This company makes audacious, overly ambitious games that don't entirely work but also won't leave my head at the very least. I didn't love playing Ancestors, but I still think of it quite regularly when one of its ideas strikes me as being intriguing or under-explored elsewhere.
And similarly I was in the Wallace Collection last week when a friend and I stumbled across Pieter de Hooch's A Boy Bringing Bread. We were both captivated by this scene, which uses a series of rectangles to recreate the interior of a Dutch household where a child has come to the door and is being greeted by a woman. Inside the house you sense a cool, spare elegance. A nearby chair has a cushion on it, and art hangs from the walls. But out through the door you can see a stretch of tiling, an arch, and another house across the street, where another figure, perhaps the boy's mother, is waiting for him.
It's one of those paintings that opens out the past and encourages you to imagine what it would be like to step onto its streets. And in 1666: Amsterdam, you can kind of do that.

Image credit: S-Game News by Connor Makar Reporter Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 11:35 a.m. 18 comments Follow Black Myth: Wukong Prioritise us on Google As the western video games industry continues to struggle, the Chinese industry appears to be booming, revealing a worth of more than $50bn in 2025 - more than five times the industry in the UK.
Niko Partners, a video game research company, released a report breaking down the staggering growth of the Chinese video game industry on its website. It found that in 2025, the Chinese market generated around $51.8bn in revenue.
To compare, the British video game market brought in $8.76bn in 2025 according to UKIE, the country's national video game association and trade body. China's 2025 performance is an astounding figure, one that marks a continued rise in prominence for the nation's video game industry.
Niko Partners forecasts that the Chinese market will keep growing, rising 4 percent in 2026 to $53.9bn. Looking further to 2030, the company predicts it'll reach $59.8bn. The reason for this growth has been driven by stronger-than-expected performance for both new and evergreen games (think live service games like Genshin Impact). An example of this can be seen with Where Winds Meet, a 2025 MMO that quickly surpassed 2 million players globally within a day of its release.
This same report from Niko Partners provided some additional insight into how Chinese gamers were interacting with the medium. It states that 46.5 percent were engaged with esports to some degree, with that figure expected to rise to 51.3 percent in 2026. 80 percent of gamers have played a mini-game, with 20 percent of total spending coming from these mini-games. These are defined as games you don't have to download: think browser games and the like.
As for important trends that may impact the future of China, Niko Partners believes generative AI's integration into game development is one factor. Back in 2025, Niko Partners found that 39 percent of Chinese gamers were interested in the gen AI's integration in games, while 60 percent of studios were already using it in development. This stands in contrast to western audiences, who continue to resist generative AI on artistic integrity, copyright, and general quality lines.
Other factors include growth in niche and underserved genres, increased out-of-app monetisation, and rising consumer spending both domestically and internationally will be key. So too will a "more favourable regulatory environment" for game developers, which Niko Partners believes should allow international game companies to access the Chinese market via platforms like Steam.
For a glimpse at how things are picking up in China from the development side, Gamescom flaunted big-hitters from the country on the show floor. Phantom Blade Zero, A Whisper of Fall: Jinyiwei, Sea of Remnants, Showa: American Story and more made an appearance, with over 60 in total having a presence at the show. The country has inarguably come a long way since Black Myth: Wukong made an astounding impact back in 2024.

News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 10:19 a.m. 10 comments Follow Onimusha: Way of the Sword Prioritise us on Google If you were hoping Onimusha: Way of the Sword would revive the dormant series, you may get your wish. Capcom today announced the latest installment in the action game series has already sold over one million copies across all platforms.
Onimusha: Way of the Sword sold that many in its first day of release, according to Capcom. The game was released on 4th September on PC, PS5, Xbox Series X/S and Switch 2. The Onimusha series as a whole has now surpassed 10 million copies sold over its lifetime.
Although Capcom hasn't shared specific sales figures for each platform, it's safe to say PC has been one of Way of the Sword's biggest. Over on Steam, the game peaked at 85,081 concurrent players (via SteamDB), and ranks among the best-selling games on the platform at the moment.
Way of the Sword is the first new release in the Onimusha series in over 20 years. The game continues Capcom's trend of successfully modernising its classic games and franchises.
By comparison, the long-in-development Pragmata sold one million copies in its first two days on sale - a good result for a new IP. Capcom's biggest hit this year so far, of course, has been Resident Evil Requiem, which sold five million units in under a week.
In July, Capcom brought forward Way of the Sword's release date, just days after the publisher-developer said it was committed to the game's previously announced 25th September release date.
In the Eurogamer review of Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Dom Peppiatt was particularly impressed with what the developer successfully crafted: a deep game of swordplay and a lack of common Soulslike design tropes.

Image credit: Eurogamer News by Connor Makar Reporter Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 9:30 a.m. 3 comments Follow 2XKO Prioritise us on Google Marc Merrill - one of the co-founders of Riot Games and its current CPO - has spoken about the in-development MMO, describing it as "the grail" following the sudden end-of-development announcement for its fighting game 2XKO.
Speaking at Pax West 2026 with Greg Miller, Merrill spoke for around an hour about Riot Games' history and future projects. This included a brief exchange around its in-development MMO at the studio, as well as the soon-to-be shuttered free-to-play fighting game Riot released earlier this year.
"We know what players' hopes and dreams are," Merrill said. "It's just on us as a team and as people to succeed in the execution. What a worthy quest. We jokingly call it the grail internally because we're like 'f*ck it, many a brave knight are going to die'."
"But f*ck it, it's the grail so lets go. That's the mindset that we really try to cultivate, but it's really hard to do at scale. But I think we're doing a reasonable job and the future is incredibly bright."
This MMO, which has yet to be given a name (even a known project name), a release window, or even a confirmation on what sort of MMO it will be, has been in development for some time. Initially under the watchful eye of former Blizzard lead Greg Street, who left the company back in 2023, the project restarted development in the past few years. Merrill has previously said the game will be out before 2030, but precious little else about the project publicly.
This statement received an interesting response online. While some expressed excitement around the project despite the crumbs of information out there, many are skeptical of the project given the recent end-of-service announcement for its recently released fighting game 2XKO. A rising sentiment appears to be 'how can we trust this game will stick around?'
"They hyping up this MMO like they aren’t just going to shoot it in the face after six months cause it won’t be bigger than WoW," writes user Sloth on X. Another user, Red Riot Ross echoed similar sentiments, writing: "The only thing 2XKO sunsetting has done for riot is give laughably bad optics on anything they do/make going forward." Tsuki, another X user, posted: "Wait till they hear how FF14's first 3 years went," a reference to the rocky start Square Enix's MMO had before the game's rise to popularity with the 'A Realm Reborn' mulligan.
Riot when their MMO doesn't have half the player base and micro transactions of FF14/Wow in 3 minutes and 39 seconds after launch. https://t.co/BxMY9KDuC2 pic.twitter.com/pLY6Tj0mAW
There are others expressing frustration at the lack of information out there about this much-hyped MMO, another parallel to 2XKO which spent a lengthy portion of its almost 10-year development time in the dark. One member of the public Snowbird wrote: "Almost seven years since they announced they were working on an MMO and we don't have a screenshot, a piece of concept art, nothin." Enderspider feels similarly, writing: "I know it's a lot of work building an MMO but it's kinda wild how we have genuinely not seen or heard anything about it besides 'we're building an MMO' despite them having worked on this for five years already now. Nothing. No snippets, no teasers, no concept art, not even a name."
Merrill did speak about 2XKO while at Pax, emphasising he "wouldn't characterize 2XKO as a mistake" despite its short life span. "One of the challenges with free-to-play games and the live service model in general… Unless you do something so incredible in a really competitive world where 20,000+ games are published a year on Steam, and there's an infinite amount of social media content, and an infinite amount of stuff to watch on YouTube, what we're doing is competing for people's attention. That's a really high bar.
"You have to do so many things right to get enough critical mass to build the community and have it turn into something and be sustainable in the long run," said Merrill. "2XKO unfortunately didn't do that, but that doesn't mean it's not a great game. That's why we're refunding. It's also why we're keeping the game live. It doesn't mean the intention to serve the fighting game community was not utterly in the hearts of the Cannons, and the Rioter's, and us the entire time.
"We're not gonna bat 1,000, but that doesn't mean we're not proud of it, and it doesn't mean we're not going to take big swings. That's another thing, I know a lot of other people are like 'oh my god I'm concerned about what this means for all sorts of other games', and it's like, well you shouldn't be. If there's one thing about Riot, [we have] an unquenchable desire to serve and make it better, and we're constantly trying to find ways to do that. We've got a lot of cool things in the pipeline."
Riot Games appears to have found itself in an interesting spot. While 2XKO is the latest in its stumbles as a massive live service games company, it is not the only one it has had to contend with. The digital card game Legends of Runeterra faced a similar fate to 2XKO back in 2024, the company cut its indie publishing label Riot Forge back around the same time. Its top-down action game Project F, which we only saw once alongside the would-be 2XKO many years ago, hasn't been seen since. While the company still has League of Legends, Teamfight Tactics, and the newly popular Riftbound TCG out and about, it's got far from a spotless history.
The pressure is on then, to prove not only that this upcoming MMO (whatever it is) can stand up in a fiercely competitive genre and be supported for the long haul. Whether Riot Games can do that remains to be seen, as does the game itself.
