Image credit: Eurogamer Preview by Dom Peppiatt Deputy Editorial Director Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 9 a.m. 46 comments Follow Fable (2026) Prioritise us on Google Fable Developer: Playground Games Publisher:Xbox Game Studios Platform: Launches on Xbox Series X/S, PlayStation 5, PC, and Nintendo Switch 2. Availability: Out 23rd February 2027. "We don't want to spoil anything," associate game director Will Kennedy as I started my much-anticipated Fable preview at Gamescom this year, "but we've got two very different loadouts for you to play with today." So began the hour-long, behind-closed-doors demo, the first time anyone outside Playground Studios has been allowed to take the long-anticipated fantasy RPG for a spin. Turns out, this little slice of the game - taken from a dungeon a little way into the game filled with undead - was quite short. But that didn't matter because the devs, smirking, told me from the outset that I'd be going through the whole thing twice. They were confident, and after playing it those two times I can tell you they were right to be.
Longtime Fable fans will instantly understand the cadence of combat Playground is going for - you need to alternate melee, ranged, and magic attacks in order to hold off the undead hordes. You can be as inelegant as you like, if that's your style: stumble into heavy melee attacks (hold button to charge), or chain together quick combos and then pelt your enemies with disjointed spells.
But, as far as I could tell from my dual demos, the real satisfaction is going to come from weaving all these individual strands together. I was locked into using a hammer in my playthrough (though I'm reliably informed that there'll be more primary weapons in the full game), and this was a nice brute force way to smack armoured skeletons around. You want to use your spells to crowd control, use melee when they get too close, and use your ranged attacks to keep enemy archers and mages at bay. When the action gets too close, you've got a block and - praise be! - a parry, too. I used this a lot to basically render any melee-enemies inert until my magic charges refilled. Resultantly, if you can think ahead and have any sense of rhythm whatsoever, you can control the pace of the fight, even if the enemy numbers threaten to overwhelm you.
During playthrough one, I could target multiple enemies in range with a lightning spell that would chain to nearby enemies. When I cast this whilst in water, it seemed to extend the reach of the spell to anyone in the pool with me. I had a spell that turned all enemies in range into chickens, and if I hit them with a fireball afterwards - you guessed it - I was suddenly surrounded by roast chicken. Very Fable.
On the second playthrough, I was given an over-powered character, equipped with late-game items and spells - the most destructive of which was a repeater crossbow. In the first demo, I'd been popping headshots with the bow - which will feel familiar to anyone that's used a bow in any third-person adventure game, ever - but the crossbow was more interesting. Packing more of a punch, it punished you with more recoil. Understandable. But the result of this was less accurate fire on my behalf, resulting in me kneecapping skeletons and so on. The first go around, anyone I popped a headshot on began swinging swords or shooting crossbow bolts randomly, liberated from the use of their eyes. In the second go, the legless foes would roll and crawl around - still dangerous but severely handicapped. Will this level of nuance be available to other enemies? Does the game's obsession with choice and agency extend to other enemy mobs, other biomes? I asked Kennedy this, and he just smiled at me.
The spells were different on the second go, too. Instead of thunder/fire/chicken, I had a spell that could lift all the enemies into the air - ripe for picking off with ranged attacks or electrifying the terrain - before slamming them back down again. I also had a sort-of 'Force Push' move that synergised nicely with the lift, a combination that cleared mobs away when I was getting overwhelmed. And I needed that breathing space the second time, because associate game director Craig Little came over between demos and bumped me up to the highest difficulty going. Cheers, mate. Here, the parry timing was tighter, the mobs hit harder, took more strategy to kill, and seemed to me to be smarter, too (this is hard to gauge in the time I had to play, though).
Both runs culminated in a boss: a 'Lantern Wraith' that took a mechanic from the rest of the level - skeletons don't just die when you defeat them, they let a wraith loose that must be eliminated unless it reanimates the corpse of a downed sack of bones - and drew it to its natural conclusion. Namely, the boss could summon wraiths that, in turn, summoned more dead. Again, very Fable. The boss itself was an extension of what these demos were trying to teach me: use melee, use your bow, use magic. Hit the weak spots, beat the mobs, profit. It's not exactly ground-breaking, but when the realtime decision-making and tools at your disposal are this meaty, I'm not going to complain.
I need to give a special shoutout to Matt King, here, too: you may know him better as Peep Show's Super Hans. Whilst the party-loving "musician" might have been pretty one-note in Peep Show, King really shows his acting chops here - the timing, delivery, and self-awareness of his character in Fable is excellent. I'm told he's one of many companions you'll get to hang out with during the game, but I really hope we see much, much more of him. I think you'll be surprised how emotive and dramatic he can be, even when cracking fart jokes and swinging a sword at skeletons.
Chris has already spoken at length about Fable's preoccupation with player choice, with how Playground has drilled into the minutiae of game development in order to furnish us the level of agency you'd expect from a Fable title. It seems what is writ large in macro is also applied to the micro, then: the moment-to-moment choice in combat is as broad and satisfying as what the studio is planning at the higher town-, city-, and world-level. There was some hesitation about the game's length over the weekend, but - having played only a sliver - I really don't think there's much need to worry. If the game promises this much depth and nuance all the way through, I don't mind playing 20 hours a few times over. This tactic clearly worked on me in the Gamescom demo, after all.

News by Sherif Saed Senior Contributor Published on Sept. 7, 2026, 8:43 a.m. 43 comments Follow The Blood of Dawnwalker Prioritise us on Google It may not surprise you to learn that The Blood of Dawnwalker's most contentious mechanic can already be removed. If you're unfamiliar, the open-world role-playing game has a time mechanic where every quest you complete pushes time forwards and uses up a little more of your 30 day, 30 night time limit (of sorts).
Time management is a core part of The Blood of Dawnwalker, so you're forced to make difficult choices across its world, knowing that doing one thing may prevent you from doing another further down the line. A lot of people clearly don't like timers, especially in open-world games where they like to do everything, which is probably why the game's most popular mod on Nexus Mods at the moment is one that eliminates it.
The Better Story Timer mod has been downloaded over 115,000 times since it went live shortly after the game's launch last week. As the mod's description notes, it "allows you to have as many days as you want for the story", and removes time costs associated with spending skill points.
By default, the mod increases the number of days for the game's main quest to 90 in-game days, triple that of the standard 30. This can be adjusted further by tweaking an ini file. The mod also increases the number of segments - chunks of the day - on the in-game clock, meaning you can do more each day. This is especially useful when acquiring skills, as some upgrades require a segment to learn, and some more powerful ones, one or two segments, which further eats into your time.
If you feel even that is not enough, the mod also lets you remove the time costs associated with learning active and passive skills without affecting other time-advancing events such as quests.
The mod has been updated to keep pace with Dawnwalker's own patches, so it should be compatible with the latest version of the game. The mod's creator notes that some people have already finished the game with it installed. It works in the much more time-limited prologue, too, but the author suggests removing it before playing the game's epilogue.
The Blood of Dawnwalker developer Rebel Wolves - made up of many Witcher and CD Projekt Red alumni - recently announced the game has sold over one million copies in just three days, and its Steam player numbers alone are healthy.
In the Eurogamer review of The Blood of Dawnwalker, Bertie praised the game's bravery for tackling an open-world RPG with new ideas, such as the time mechanic, and was enormously encouraged by the game, even if it didn't quite hang together in parts.

Image credit: Saber Interactive / Unigine News by Vikki Blake Contributor Published on Sept. 6, 2026, 3:40 p.m. 30 comments Follow Rideshare "Stimulator" Prioritise us on Google Saber Interactive CCO Tim Willits has confirmed the company has not revised its communications strategy despite its CEO telling the press that he "would [...] have been happy to replace [a writer] with AI" after she claimed she was replaced by ChatGPT.
CEO Matthew Karch has since apologised to Stella Sacco, the writer at the centre of the Rideshare Stimulator AI controversy, but not before widespread public condemnation. He also shared a statement saying he'd had an "insightful week" but "the digital ecosystem thrives on outrage and surface-level takes".
"Sometimes we 'say what we mean' too much," Willits told PC Gamer, reflecting on the blunt comms from the studio's leadership.
When PC Gamer pressed directly on whether the recent backlash had prompted reflection, he reportedly said "no".
"I've been in the industry for so long, and there's always some dust up. People got mad at Saber because we put World War Z on Epic, and people were like, 'oh, Saber's destroying the industry'," Willits added.
"Now 30 million people have played World War Z. And the games will speak for themselves, even in our experiment with Rideshare [Stimulator]."
He closed by encouraging people to "check it out when it comes out" and play it themselves.
"They may be like, 'Oh, this is cool! I like this,' you know. And if they don't like it, fine," he added.
"We are going to stick to making the best games we can. Try to show them, give people an opportunity to play them, and have players make their own decisions because players are smart, you know. You make a good game, they'll find it and play it."
In a separate interview with Eurogamer, Willits said that in an era marked by long periods of little output from studios between big releases, Saber's confidence seems so high right now, Willits believes "we can get any IP".
The studio has finally added the AI disclaimer to Rideshare Stimulator's Steam page that had been conspicuously missing since the game first went live for wishlisting on 30th July. Initially, Karch said the disclaimer would come "once [the game was] finalised", but the store has since been updated to include the AI disclosure.
Saber Interactive currently has multiple games in development, including Turok Origins and Clive Barker's Hellraiser: Revival, both having a presence at Gamescom. The studio is also working on Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 3, though we've not heard much about that project since its announcement.

Image credit: Double Fine News by Vikki Blake Contributor Published on Sept. 6, 2026, 3:07 p.m. 12 comments Follow Thank You Bus Driver Prioritise us on Google Double Fine's first game in its new post-Xbox era is Thank You Bus Driver.
Described as a comedy simulation game, the game - listed only as "coming soon" on Steam - sees you take on the role of a "reckless" bus driver in which you're encouraged to "drive fast, slap faster, and toss any rulebreakers out of your bus to reach true victory: being appreciated".
You can see the chaos for yourself below:
"Take on the role of a town’s rules-driven (and reckless) bus driver in Thank You Bus Driver!" the Steam description teases.
"Getting to your next stop is all that matters. That might mean pulling up your map mid-turn or it might mean a shortcut through the corn field. Avoiding pedestrians, incoming traffic, or the fence directly in front of you is optional."
Thank You Bus Driver is available to pre-order now on Steam and GOG.
Double Fine has, of course, recently come out the other side of Xbox's restructuring. Xbox's wider reorganisation, announced by CEO Asha Sharma in July, affected around 3,200 roles across the division and saw several studios, including Double Fine, spun back out into independence while keeping hold of their IP and back catalogues. Compulsion Games, the We Happy Few and South of Midnight studio, also cut loose from Xbox in the same restructuring and has similarly confirmed it retains ownership of its IP.
Double Fine itself laid off roughly a quarter of its 90-person team as part of the transition, saying at the time that the cuts were needed to reach "a size that we can sustain".

Image credit: Valve News by Vikki Blake Contributor Published on Sept. 6, 2026, 12:42 p.m. 2 comments Follow Left 4 Dead 2 Prioritise us on Google Valve itself "leaked" the 2009 Left 4 Dead 2 trailer.
That's according to former Valve writer Chet Faliszek, who revealed in a recent video about lines cut from the game that the developer had clashed with the ratings board over the game's violence, gore, and profanity.
"For Left 4 Dead 2 with the ESRB… we leaked our trailer ahead of time because they wouldn't let us release the trailer," he said in the video below (thanks, Ars Technica).
"You have to remember... Valve was in fights with the ESRB, with Australia, with Germany, with a bunch of countries about the profanity in the game, the violence," Faliszek said.
"I'll just admit that [we leaked the trailer]. I think we can't get in trouble for that now. It's like 20 years ago."
Valve had already clashed with the ESRB earlier that same year over an early promotional image that showed a hand with three fingers gnawed off, leaving two intact to signal the sequel number. The ESRB objected, and Valve had to rework the image to the one we now know, which has the missing fingers merely curled under instead.
Around the same time, the ratings board had also forced D3's Dark Sector and 2K's The Darkness to remove trailers that had already circulated behind age gates, arguing the content was likely to "cause serious offense to the average consumer".
So instead of submitting the Left 4 Dead 2 trailer for approval, Valve seeded it as an unofficial leak. The footage later became the game's actual intro cinematic and Left 4 Dead 2 received an M rating, sidestepping the more restrictive AO rating handed to Manhunt 2 two years earlier.
Left 4 Dead 2 was released in 2009, but it took until 2021 for the first-person zombie shooter to be released in Germany after it was pulled from sale shortly after launch. Over a decade after Left 4 Dead 2 came out, Valve requested the German authorities re-evaluate the zombie shooter, and as a result, the uncut international version was finally made available in the country.
